draft.title: Reference words and cohesion
card: Cohesion is how the sentences in a text link together so it reads as one piece. A reference word helps by pointing back to something already said.

Words such as this, that, these, those, such, it and they stand in for an earlier idea. Writers use them so they do not repeat the same words. Example: "The council banned plastic bags. This reduced litter."
Reference words need a clear target. In "Tom met Ravi, and he laughed", the word he could mean either boy, so the link is unclear.
The former and the latter point back to two things named earlier. The former is the first one named, and the latter is the second one named.
draft.remember: A reference word points back to an earlier idea, so sentences link without repeats, but the target must be clear.

a.q: Read: "Many schools have started later. These changes help tired teenagers." What does the word These do?
opts: Points back to the schools' earlier starts
Adds a new fact about teenagers
Introduces a new topic for the text
Repeats the first sentence word for word
a.why: These points back to the idea in the first sentence, so the two sentences link. It does not add a new fact or topic, and it does not repeat the first sentence, because it only stands in for the idea.
a.clue: Ask what idea the word sends you back to.

b.q: Read: "Mia met Zoe, and she gave her a gift." What is the main problem with the reference words?
opts: She and her could each point to either girl
The word and should be replaced with a full stop
There are no reference words to link the sentence
The former should be used instead of the gift
b.why: Both she and her could mean Mia or Zoe, so a reader cannot tell who gave the gift to whom. The sentence does have reference words, so saying it has none is wrong.
b.clue: Check whether each pointing word has one clear target.

a.best: Points back to the schools' earlier starts

b.best: She and her could each point to either girl

problems.detail: The right option says 'the schools' earlier starts', but the sentence says the schools have started later. A student could read 'earlier starts' as starting earlier, the opposite of the text. Better wording: 'Points back to the schools starting later'.
